design_detail: Cross-sectional family study (a Science report without section headings, with a 12-page Supporting Online Material). 50 pairs of full biological siblings recruited in East Anglia, UK, in each of which one sibling met DSM-IV-TR criteria for cocaine or amphetamine dependence and the other had no personal history of substance dependence except nicotine (the supplement's enrolment criterion; the main report says no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse), compared with 50 unrelated healthy volunteers without a personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence. Measures: stop-signal reaction time (SSRT); white-matter fractional anisotropy (FA) from diffusion tensor imaging, analysed with tract-based spatial statistics and permutation tests with threshold-free cluster enhancement; grey-matter volume by voxel-based morphometry in FSL, compared with the controls by cluster-level permutation tests in CamBA, the regions shared by both sibling groups being the overlap of the two comparisons. Familiality was tested by permutation: whether a measure differed less within true sibling pairs than when each dependent participant was paired at random with an unrelated sibling (one-tailed). Recorded as cross-sectional rather than case-control (the abstract-based draft) because participants were selected on dependence status, the exposure, and compared at a single time. The main report (pp. 601–604) and the Supporting Online Material (12 pages: methods, figs. S1–S2, tables S1–S3, references) were read in full, tables and figures on rendered pages. Locators in the report count its running-text paragraphs from the first one after the abstract; pages of the supplement are cited by its own printed page numbers (pp. 2–12; p. 1 is its cover).
can_establish: Whether stop-signal and brain-structure differences seen in people with stimulant dependence are also present in their siblings who were not dependent, and whether these traits are more alike within families than between unrelated people, which points to a familial (genetic or shared-environment) component.
cannot_establish: That the shared differences predate drug use in the dependent siblings (nobody was assessed before use began); that they are genetic rather than due to the shared family environment (siblings share both); that stimulant use has no effect of its own (shared differences could still be worsened by use, and neither the report nor the supplement compares the dependent with the non-dependent siblings directly); that the differences are not partly due to tobacco (55% of the siblings and 12% of the controls smoked, and only grey matter was re-analysed in non-smokers); or anything specific to methamphetamine (94% of the dependent participants were dependent on cocaine and 6% on amphetamines, and methamphetamine is not mentioned).

sample.recruitment: By advertisements and from treatment services in the East Anglia region of the UK; all recruits were assessed with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SOM p. 2). The acknowledgments thank the clinical study officers of the Mental Health Research Network for help with volunteer recruitment (p. 604). How many dependent participants came from treatment services, and whether they were in treatment when tested, is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Sibling pairs: same biological parents; one sibling met DSM-IV-TR criteria for cocaine or amphetamine dependence; the other had no personal history of substance dependence except nicotine (SOM p. 2; the main report describes the siblings as having no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, p. 602). Controls: no personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence. All participants aged 18–55 and able to read and write English. Excluded in all groups: lifetime psychotic disorder, neurological illness, neurodevelopmental disorder or traumatic head injury (SOM p. 2). Dependence on other drugs and psychiatric disorders other than psychosis are not listed among the exclusions.
sample.demographics: Table S1 (SOM p. 8; 50 controls, 49 non-dependent siblings, 47 dependent siblings): men 64%, 51% and 92% (chi-square 19.0, P < 0.001); age 32.8 (SD 8.9), 32.6 (8.4) and 34.5 (7.4) years (P = 0.702); verbal IQ (NART) 112.3, 108.9 and 110.3 (P = 0.143); education 12.6, 12.1 and 11.6 years (P = 0.062); current smokers 12%, 55% and 94% (P < 0.001). Upbringing shared until age 10 for 90% of the non-dependent and 92% of the dependent siblings, and until 15 for 75% and 89%. The supplement calls the groups relatively well matched in age, IQ and education but different in sex, because most dependent participants were men (SOM p. 2); no individual matching is described.
sample.attrition: Of 154 people enrolled, 150 completed the study (three groups of 50). MRI scans were unavailable for three dependent participants and one sibling, leaving 146 for grey matter (47, 49 and 50), and one more dependent participant could not tolerate a full session, leaving 145 for white matter (46, 49 and 50) (SOM pp. 2, 4). Why the four scans were unavailable, and how many complete pairs entered the familiality tests, is not stated (at most 47 for grey matter and 46 for white matter, editors' calculation). The degrees of freedom of the FA comparison fit 145 participants with sex as a covariate; those of the SSRT comparison do not fit the 146 of Table S1 (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Families in which a sibling without substance dependence agreed to take part beside a dependent sibling: dependent people with such a sibling may differ from those without, and the non-dependent siblings are a selected group (the authors suggest they have resilience factors, p. 604). Recruitment was by advertisement and through treatment services. Controls had no personal or family history of dependence, so the comparison with them contrasts families with and without dependence, as intended, but also any other way in which such families differ. The groups differed in sex (51% and 64% men among non-dependent siblings and controls, 92% among dependent siblings) and in smoking (55% and 12%; 94%).

exposure.measurement: DSM-IV-TR diagnosis on the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV, given to all participants (SOM p. 2). The dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine (94%) or amphetamines (6%; which amphetamines is not stated, and methamphetamine is not mentioned) (SOM p. 2). Urine was positive for stimulants in all but three of them; the urine screens of all non-dependent siblings and controls were drug-negative. Drug and alcohol use were screened with the DAST-20 and the AUDIT (SOM p. 2; Table S1, p. 8). The main report names only DSM-IV dependence on stimulant drugs (p. 602); a later review states that most participants used cocaine (Dean et al., 2013, p. 263).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mean 16.3 years (SD 7.6) of stimulant use, from a mean age of 16.5 (SD 2.8) (SOM p. 2). Frequency, amount and route are not reported. Duration of use appears as a correlate within the dependent group in maps only (Fig. S2, SOM p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Most dependent siblings also met criteria for dependence on another substance: opiates 55%, alcohol 26%, cannabis 9% (SOM p. 2); their mean AUDIT score was 11.4 (SD 11.4), against 3.3 in controls and 3.9 in non-dependent siblings (Table S1, p. 8). Current smokers: 94% of dependent siblings, 55% of non-dependent siblings, 12% of controls. The non-dependent siblings' drug use was minimal (DAST-20 mean 0.5, SD 1.1, against 0.0 in controls; drug-negative urine), and their alcohol use did not differ from the controls' (t(70.9) = −0.72, P = 0.472) (SOM pp. 2–3, 8). Tobacco was addressed only for grey matter, by a re-analysis restricted to non-smoking controls and non-dependent siblings (Fig. S1, SOM p. 6; numbers and statistics not given); no smoking check is reported for FA or SSRT.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not abstinent: the dependent siblings were still using stimulants (urine positive for stimulants in all but three), were not asked to abstain because withdrawal may impair performance, and were screened only for intoxication severe enough to incapacitate them; alcohol was not breathalysed. The assessment session took place about 4 hours before scanning, and the stop-signal task was done after the scans (SOM pp. 2–3). The authors argue, citing another study, that recent cocaine use would if anything improve stop-signal performance (SOM p. 3).

comparison.controls: 50 unrelated healthy volunteers without a personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence (p. 602; SOM p. 2); within families, the non-dependent biological siblings.
comparison.matching: The main report says the controls were matched for age and IQ (p. 602); the supplement shows similar group means for age, verbal IQ and education and describes no individual matching; sex differed (Table S1, SOM p. 8). Sex was a covariate in the analyses of demographic and stop-signal data (SOM p. 3), and grey-matter comparisons restricted to men or to women are said not to have changed the results (SOM p. 4; no statistics).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No assessment before drug use began in the dependent siblings. The non-dependent sibling stands in for the pre-use state, which assumes that both siblings started alike; genes and the shared family environment (for example adversity or parental substance use) are not separated. Upbringing was shared until age 10 for about 90% of the pairs and until 15 for 75–89% (Table S1, SOM p. 8). Childhood adversity, parental substance use and psychiatric history other than psychosis are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Non-dependent siblings: no personal history of substance dependence except nicotine; occasional use is not excluded, but their DAST-20 scores were very low (mean 0.5) and their urine was drug-negative; 55% smoked. Controls: no personal or family history of dependence, DAST-20 0.0, AUDIT 3.3, drug-negative urine, 12% smokers (SOM pp. 2, 8).

outcomes.instruments: Stop-signal task (SSRT); diffusion tensor imaging with tract-based spatial statistics (FA) and voxel-based morphometry (grey-matter volume) in FSL; a right inferior frontal and pre-supplementary motor region of interest from Hammers' probabilistic atlas for the FA–SSRT regression; permutation tests of within-pair similarity (p. 602). Supplement: stop-signal task of five blocks of 64 trials, 75% go trials, stop-signal timing set by a tracking algorithm (SOM p. 3); MRI on a 3T Siemens TIM Trio, T1-weighted MPRAGE (1 mm slices) and diffusion-weighted EPI with 63 directions (b = 1000 s/mm²), all images screened by a neuroradiologist (SOM p. 4); grey matter by FSL-VBM (modulated partial-volume images, smoothed at 2.3 mm FWHM) with permutation testing in CamBA; FA by TBSS with randomise (SOM pp. 4–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: SSRT is a standard laboratory measure of response inhibition; it is compared with the control group, not with norms. The imaging measures are group-relative.
outcomes.operationalization: An abnormality is a difference from the unrelated controls; a difference is called familial when the variance of the within-pair differences is smaller in true sibling pairs than when each dependent participant is paired at random with an unrelated sibling (100,000 re-pairings, one-tailed test; SOM p. 5); impaired self-control means a longer SSRT than the controls.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Three outcome measures (SSRT, FA, grey-matter volume), the last two tested voxel by voxel. SSRT: Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons (P ≤ 0.005 for both sibling groups against controls; Fig. 1A legend; SOM p. 3). FA: three-group permutation F test and two-group t tests with threshold-free cluster enhancement (5000 permutations), maps corrected for multiple comparisons at P < 0.05 (SOM p. 5). Grey matter: cluster-level permutation threshold set at one expected false-positive cluster per map (cluster-wise P of 9 × 10⁻⁴ for non-dependent siblings and 8 × 10⁻⁴ for dependent siblings against controls), giving four and eight clusters; the shared regions are the overlap of the two maps, which use the same control group (SOM p. 4). The six familiality tests are one-tailed (SOM p. 5) and reported without correction; editors' calculation: across six tests a Bonferroni threshold would be P < 0.0083, which the SSRT (0.033), putamen (0.013) and posterior insula (0.012) results do not meet.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the imaging analyses are automated, and FA maps were inspected visually for registration errors (SOM p. 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: SSRT (Table S1, SOM p. 8): 238.9 ms (SD 45.0) in controls, 276.7 (55.5) in non-dependent siblings and 280.8 (61.9) in dependent siblings, F = 8.9, P < 0.001 (the main report gives F(2,141) = 9.9, P < 0.001; see reporting issues); both sibling groups slower than controls (Bonferroni P ≤ 0.005). FA (Table S2, SOM p. 9; means over the 24,934 skeleton voxels that differed between groups): 0.55 (SD 0.02) in controls, 0.53 (0.02) in non-dependent siblings and 0.52 (0.02) in dependent siblings, F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001 (p. 602); right inferior frontal gyrus (317 such voxels) 0.51, 0.49 and 0.48 (SD 0.03); mean diffusivity across the skeleton 710, 712 and 730 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s. Grey matter in the shared clusters (Table S2): left amygdala (984 mm³) 0.76, 0.81 and 0.83 (SD 0.07); left putamen (560 mm³) 0.34, 0.38 and 0.38 (SD 0.05–0.06); left postcentral gyrus (1,152 mm³) 0.89, 0.75 and 0.74 (SD 0.11–0.12). FA beside the right inferior frontal gyrus against SSRT, all participants pooled: r = 0.24 printed without sign (negative by the text and Fig. 1C), R² = 0.057, P < 0.005 (p. 602). Familiality (one-tailed permutation tests): SSRT P = 0.033; FA P = 0.004; right prefrontal white matter P = 0.004; putamen P = 0.013; posterior insula P = 0.012; amygdala P = 0.144 (not familial). Editors' calculations: SSRT standardized differences from controls about 0.75 (non-dependent siblings) and 0.78 (dependent siblings), pooled SD about 50–54 ms; grey matter, non-dependent siblings against controls about 0.7 (amygdala), 0.7 (putamen) and 1.2 (postcentral) SD, dependent siblings against controls about 1.0, 0.8 and 1.3 SD; FA about 1 and 1.5 SD, very approximate because the FA means and SDs are printed to two decimals; eta-squared from F(2,141) = 26.3 about 0.27. All the imaging values are means over voxels selected because they differed between groups, so these differences are inflated by the selection and are not effect sizes for the regions; the SSRT differences are not affected by selection.
analysis.covariates: Sex was a covariate in the analyses of covariance of demographic and stop-signal data, with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests (SOM p. 3); whether it was also a covariate in the FA comparison is not stated (F(2,141) for 145 participants fits one covariate, editors' calculation). Grey matter: comparisons restricted to men or to women are said not to change the results (SOM p. 4), and a re-analysis of non-smoking controls and non-dependent siblings kept the three regions (Fig. S1, SOM p. 6); neither gives statistics. No covariates (such as age, sex or total brain volume) are described for the voxel-wise maps or for the familiality tests.
analysis.selective_reporting: The main report names only the grey-matter clusters shared by both sibling groups; the supplement adds that the comparison with controls gave four clusters for the non-dependent and eight for the dependent siblings (SOM p. 4) but names none beyond the three shared regions. Fig. 2A shows decreased-volume clusters in the dependent group, in ventral frontal and insular regions by the editors' reading of the figure, that are absent from the siblings' map (Fig. 2B), and Fig. 2B shows large increased-volume clusters in the posterior fossa of the siblings (the cerebellum, by the editors' reading); neither is named or discussed. The FA two-group t tests (SOM p. 5) are not reported, and no direct comparison of the dependent with the non-dependent siblings is reported for any measure. The single-sex and non-smoker re-analyses and the correlations with duration of use are given without statistics (SOM pp. 4, 6–7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Both siblings of each pair had longer SSRT than unrelated controls (about 277 and 281 against 239 ms) and lower white-matter FA (0.53 and 0.52 against 0.55, in voxels selected for differing), and they shared three grey-matter differences from the controls (larger left amygdala and left putamen; smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula). SSRT, FA, right prefrontal FA, putamen and posterior insula varied less within families than in random pairings (one-tailed, uncorrected); the amygdala did not. For FA the non-dependent siblings fell between the controls and the dependent siblings; for SSRT and the putamen and postcentral clusters they did not. The supplement maps regions where FA and grey matter fell with years of stimulant use in the dependent siblings, without statistics. The dependent siblings were still using stimulants when tested, 94% were dependent on cocaine, and most were also dependent on opiates or alcohol.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings support an underlying neurocognitive endophenotype for stimulant addiction (p. 601). The text goes further: poor inhibitory control is called a familial trait and not a result of long-term drug use (p. 602), the right prefrontal FA finding is called an objective vulnerability marker (p. 602), and the grey-matter and white-matter changes are said to underlie an increased risk of dependence (p. 604). Gaps: (1) an endophenotype must be heritable, but siblings share environment as well as genes and no heritability was estimated; the authors themselves note that an equal SSRT deficit in both siblings does not fit the classic endophenotype pattern of relatives falling between patients and controls (p. 604); (2) an equal deficit in a non-dependent sibling shows that the trait is shared, not that drug use adds nothing or that the trait came first; (3) 'underlie' and 'vulnerability marker' are causal or predictive readings of cross-sectional data; (4) the marker rests on r = 0.24 (about 6% of SSRT variance) across all participants pooled, which mixes the between-group difference with individual variation; (5) the abstract speaks of fronto-striatal systems, but the grey-matter differences shared by both siblings lie in the amygdala, putamen, posterior insula and adjacent parietal and temporal cortex, and the frontal finding is white matter beside the right inferior frontal gyrus. The supplement adds that the data indicate that the putamen, amygdala/hippocampus and superior temporal gyrus/posterior insula are vulnerability markers for developing drug dependence (SOM p. 5), and that the siblings' higher smoking may be another aspect of their genetic risk rather than a confounding cause of their brain differences (SOM p. 6). Further gaps: (6) vulnerability marker for developing dependence is a predictive reading of cross-sectional data, and the smoking argument is an interpretation, not a test; the sentence after the non-smoker re-analysis, as printed, says the opposite of what the authors mean (SOM p. 6; see reporting issues); (7) the main report's statement that white-matter changes can also result from drug-taking (p. 602) rests on maps without statistics, in which years of use are not separated from age or from the dependent siblings' opiate and alcohol dependence.

timeline.event: The same group's earlier sibling study reported higher Barratt impulsivity scores and normal sensation-seeking in non-dependent siblings (Ersche et al., 2010, Biological Psychiatry, as cited on p. 604; not read).
This study: SSRT, FA and grey-matter differences shared by 50 sibling pairs discordant for stimulant dependence.
Review notes that most participants in this sibling study used cocaine rather than methamphetamine; the supplement gives 94% cocaine and 6% amphetamine dependence

Review summarizes the brain findings, adding a hippocampal enlargement in both siblings and orbitofrontal and anterior insular reductions in the dependent siblings only; the orbitofrontal and anterior insular reductions are named neither in the main report nor in the supplement, which calls the shared medial temporal cluster amygdala/hippocampus in its text and Table S3 and amygdala in Table S2 and Fig. S1

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication of this sibling design has been read for the encyclopedia; the status records the project's reading, not a search of the literature. The study is the encyclopedia's main human evidence that some brain and stop-signal differences seen in stimulant dependence are shared with non-dependent siblings; it says nothing specific about methamphetamine: 94% of the dependent participants were dependent on cocaine and the rest on amphetamines, which are not named.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective family cohort that images and tests children or adolescents before any drug use and follows them and their siblings through the ages of onset, so that differences present before use can be separated from changes after it; a twin design would also separate genetic from shared-environment effects. Meanwhile, a direct contrast of dependent with non-dependent siblings, reported with cluster statistics, would show which differences are specific to the dependent sibling. For this encyclopedia's question, the same design is needed in families of people dependent on methamphetamine, with controls matched for smoking and with the dependent siblings' other dependence measured and taken into account.

domains.note: The sibling design addresses familial and some background factors; age, verbal IQ and education were similar (Table S1). Sex differed (51% and 64% men among non-dependent siblings and controls, 92% among dependent siblings) and was a covariate in the behavioural analyses, with single-sex grey-matter analyses said not to change the results (no statistics). Smoking (55% of non-dependent siblings against 12% of controls) was checked only for grey matter, by a re-analysis of non-smokers without statistics; FA and SSRT were not checked. The dependent siblings' opiate (55%) and alcohol (26%) dependence bears on differences found only in them and on the duration correlations, not on the differences shared with the non-dependent siblings.

DSM-IV-TR diagnosis on a structured clinical interview, current use confirmed by urine in all but three dependent siblings, and drug-negative urine with very low DAST-20 scores in non-dependent siblings and controls (SOM p. 2; Table S1). The stimulant is cocaine for 94%: that is indirectness for a methamphetamine page, rated in the claim, not a measurement bias.

Recruited by advertisement and through treatment services; families with a willing non-dependent sibling, and controls without a family history of dependence. Sex and smoking differ between groups (see confounding).

The dependent siblings were tested while still using stimulants, screened only for incapacitating intoxication, so recent use or withdrawal may affect their stop-signal performance (the authors argue, from another study, that recent use would improve it); whether any were in treatment, including opioid substitution, is not reported. This does not bear on the non-dependent siblings.

154 enrolled and 150 completed; four unavailable scans and one incomplete session are reported (SOM pp. 2, 4), leaving 146 and 145 participants for grey and white matter, under 4% missing. The SSRT degrees of freedom remain unexplained (see reporting issues).
Automated imaging analyses, FA maps inspected for registration errors and all images screened by a neuroradiologist (SOM pp. 4–5); a standard computerized stop-signal task.

Only the clusters shared by both sibling groups are named (four and eight clusters were found against controls); the FA t tests between groups, the single-sex and non-smoker re-analyses and the duration correlations are given without statistics; the imaging values in Table S2 are means over voxels selected because they differed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four of seven domains raise some concerns. For the claim's key comparison, the non-dependent siblings against the controls, the most important are smoking (55% against 12%), checked only for grey matter and without statistics, so the white-matter and stop-signal similarities between the siblings may partly reflect tobacco; and a selective description of the whole-brain results, with imaging values from voxels selected because they differed and a grey-matter threshold that allows one false-positive cluster per map, the shared clusters coming from two comparisons with the same control group. The supplement resolves the first-pass concerns about unknown sex, education and other drug use and about the missing participants, which lowers two domains to low; the rating is no longer provisional. The design is a real strength for its question: differences shared with non-dependent siblings argue that part of the brain and stop-signal differences seen in stimulant dependence is familial. The study may be cited for that, with these limits; not for the claim that the differences predate use or are genetic, not for effects of years of use (shown only as maps), and not for methamphetamine specifically (94% of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine).

key_findings.finding: 50 sibling pairs, one sibling with DSM-IV stimulant dependence and the other with no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, and 50 unrelated healthy volunteers matched for age and IQ; smoking rates were higher in the sibling pairs than in the volunteers.
key_findings.locator: Report text, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Sample characteristics are in Table S1 of the supplement (SOM p. 8): smokers 55% of non-dependent siblings, 94% of dependent siblings and 12% of controls; see the findings added from the supplement.

key_findings.finding: SSRT differed between the three groups, F(2,141) = 9.9, P < 0.001; both the dependent and the non-dependent siblings were slower than the unrelated volunteers (Bonferroni P ≤ 0.005 for both), and the non-dependent siblings' deficit was as large as the dependent siblings'.
key_findings.locator: Report text, 4th paragraph; Fig. 1A and legend
key_findings.note: Table S1 gives the means: 238.9 ms (SD 45.0) in controls, 276.7 (55.5) in non-dependent siblings and 280.8 (61.9) in dependent siblings, F = 8.9, P < 0.001, for 146 participants; the F value and its degrees of freedom do not match the main report's F(2,141) = 9.9 (see reporting issues). They replace the first-pass readings from Fig. 1A (about 239, 277 and 280 ms), which agreed.

key_findings.finding: SSRT varied less within true sibling pairs than within unrelated pairs (permutation P = 0.033), which the authors take to show a familial trait rather than a result of long-term drug use.
key_findings.locator: Report text, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: White-matter FA was lower in the sibling pairs than in the unrelated volunteers (tract skeleton, F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001) and varied less within true sibling pairs (permutation P = 0.004); in the dependent siblings, lower FA went with longer duration of stimulant use (fig. S2A).
key_findings.locator: Report text, 5th paragraph; Fig. 1B legend
key_findings.note: The duration correlation is shown in Fig. S2A as a map only (SOM p. 7): regions where FA is negatively correlated with years of stimulant use, less extensive than the familial effect; no statistic, threshold or adjustment for age is given.

key_findings.finding: Across all participants, lower FA beside the right inferior frontal gyrus went with longer SSRT, r = 0.24 (R² = 0.057, about 6% of SSRT variance, P < 0.005); this right prefrontal white matter was more alike within families than between unrelated pairs (permutation P = 0.004).
key_findings.locator: Report text, 6th paragraph; Fig. 1C and legend
key_findings.note: The correlation pools all three groups, which differ in both FA and SSRT; no within-group estimate is reported.

key_findings.finding: Grey matter: the medial temporal lobe and basal ganglia were larger in the sibling pairs than in the volunteers, and three clusters were shared by both sibling groups: a larger left amygdala and left putamen, and a smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula.

key_findings.finding: The putamen enlargement (permutation P = 0.013) and the posterior insula reduction (P = 0.012) varied less within true sibling pairs than within random pairs; the amygdala enlargement did not (P = 0.144), which the authors attribute to non-familial factors.

key_findings.finding: The dependent participants met DSM-IV-TR criteria for stimulant dependence, 94% for cocaine and 6% for amphetamines; they had used stimulants for a mean of 16.3 years (SD 7.6) from a mean age of 16.5 (SD 2.8); urine was positive for stimulants in all but three; most also met criteria for dependence on another substance (opiates 55%, alcohol 26%, cannabis 9%). Urine screens of all siblings and controls were drug-negative.

key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Study sample, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Which amphetamines is not stated; methamphetamine is not mentioned anywhere in the report or the supplement. 6% of 50 is 3 people (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The dependent participants were tested while still using stimulants: they were not asked to abstain, because withdrawal can impair performance, and were screened only for intoxication severe enough to incapacitate them; alcohol was not breathalysed; the assessment session took place about 4 hours before scanning and the stop-signal task after the scans.

key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Study sample, 1st paragraph (last sentence), 4th paragraph (p. 2, continuing on p. 3) and 5th paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Table S1 (50 controls, 49 non-dependent siblings, 47 dependent siblings): men 64%, 51% and 92% (chi-square 19.0, P < 0.001); age 32.8, 32.6 and 34.5 years (P = 0.702); verbal IQ 112.3, 108.9 and 110.3 (P = 0.143); education 12.6, 12.1 and 11.6 years (P = 0.062); current smokers 12%, 55% and 94% (chi-square 71.8, P < 0.001); upbringing shared until age 10 for 90% and 92% of the two sibling groups and until 15 for 75% and 89%; DAST-20 0.0 and 0.5 (controls and non-dependent siblings; not given for the dependent group); AUDIT 3.3, 3.9 and 11.4; SSRT 238.9, 276.7 and 280.8 ms (F = 8.9, P < 0.001). Alcohol use did not differ between non-dependent siblings and controls (t(70.9) = −0.72, P = 0.472). Sex was a covariate in all analyses of demographic and stop-signal data, with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests.
key_findings.page: pp. 3, 8 of the Supporting Online Material
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Study sample, 5th paragraph, and Statistical analysis (p. 3); Table S1 (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Grey matter (146 participants): comparisons with the controls used cluster-level permutation tests thresholded at one expected false-positive cluster per map (cluster-wise P = 9 × 10⁻⁴ for siblings and 8 × 10⁻⁴ for dependent participants); they gave four clusters for the siblings and eight for the dependent participants, and the voxels in both lay in three regions; comparisons restricted to men or to women did not change the results. FA (145 participants): voxel-wise permutation F and t tests with threshold-free cluster enhancement and 5000 permutations, corrected at P < 0.05; mean FA in the significant skeleton and in atlas regions of the inferior frontal gyrus and pre-supplementary motor area were then analysed in SPSS.
key_findings.page: pp. 4–5 of the Supporting Online Material
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › MRI data processing and analyses (p. 4); DTI data processing and analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 4, continuing on p. 5) and 2nd paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Both grey-matter comparisons use the same control group, so a chance difference in the controls would appear in both and be counted as shared (editors' reasoning); the familiality test, which does not involve the controls, guards against this for the putamen and posterior insula but not for the amygdala, which failed it.

key_findings.finding: Table S2 (means and SDs): FA across the 24,934 skeleton voxels that differed between groups 0.55 (0.02) in controls, 0.53 (0.02) in non-dependent siblings and 0.52 (0.02) in dependent siblings; right inferior frontal gyrus (317 voxels) 0.51, 0.49 and 0.48 (0.03); left inferior frontal gyrus 0 voxels; pre-supplementary motor area left (156 voxels) 0.61, 0.59 and 0.58 and right (496 voxels) 0.58, 0.57 and 0.55; mean diffusivity across the skeleton 710, 712 and 730; grey matter in the left amygdala cluster (984 mm³) 0.76, 0.81 and 0.83 (0.07), left putamen (560 mm³) 0.34, 0.38 and 0.38, left postcentral gyrus (1,152 mm³) 0.89, 0.75 and 0.74.
key_findings.page: p. 9 of the Supporting Online Material
key_findings.locator: Table S2
key_findings.note: The caption says the values are for voxels that showed significant group differences, so the group differences are inflated by the selection. Editors' calculation of standardized differences from controls: grey matter about 0.7, 0.7 and 1.2 SD (non-dependent siblings) and 1.0, 0.8 and 1.3 SD (dependent siblings) for amygdala, putamen and postcentral gyrus. FA is ordered dependent < non-dependent siblings < controls, the classic endophenotype pattern (also stated in the Fig. S2A legend); SSRT, putamen and postcentral values are not.

key_findings.finding: Familiality: the variance of the within-pair differences in each measure was compared with its distribution when each dependent participant was paired at random with an unrelated sibling, over 100,000 re-pairings, as a one-tailed test at P < 0.05; no adjustment for age or sex before the test is described.
key_findings.page: p. 5 of the Supporting Online Material
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Assessment of familiality

key_findings.finding: Smoking: 12% of controls, 55% of siblings and 94% of dependent participants smoked. The authors argue that tobacco-related grey-matter changes reported elsewhere lie in other regions (Table S3) and that the siblings' higher smoking may be part of their genetic risk; a re-analysis restricted to non-smoking controls and siblings kept the amygdala, putamen and postcentral differences significant (Fig. S1). No smoking analysis is reported for white matter or SSRT, although the section heading names white matter.

key_findings.finding: Duration of use: Fig. S2 shows, in the dependent participants, white-matter regions where FA was negatively correlated with years of stimulant use (less extensive than the familial FA effect) and grey-matter regions negatively correlated with duration, in places different from the shared amygdala and putamen clusters; regions are shown only on slices, without names, statistics, threshold or correction.

key_findings.locator: Fig. S2 and legend
key_findings.note: With use starting at 16.5 (SD 2.8) years and age 34.5 (SD 7.4), years of use rise almost in step with age in this group (editors' reasoning), and no adjustment for age, or for the 55% with opiate and 26% with alcohol dependence, is described; by the editors' reading of the image, the grey-matter regions lie near the midline in ventral frontal and striatal territory.

key_findings.finding: The supplement labels the shared medial temporal cluster amygdala/hippocampus in its text and in Table S3 (peak at x = −22, y = −6, z = −16), but amygdala in Table S2 and Fig. S1; the main report says amygdala.

reporting_issues.issue: The SSRT and FA group comparisons are reported as F(2,141) (p. 602). The supplement explains the imaging numbers: 145 participants had white-matter data (SOM p. 4), and with sex as a covariate that gives 141 degrees of freedom (editors' calculation). For SSRT, Table S1 gives F = 8.9 for 146 participants (50, 49, 47), against F = 9.9 in the main report; 146 participants give 142 degrees of freedom with one covariate and 143 without (SOM pp. 3, 8).
reporting_issues.page: p. 602; pp. 3–4, 8 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: For FA the first-pass concern (six participants missing without explanation) is resolved. The SSRT comparison cannot be reproduced from either place: which participants entered it, and which F value is right, is unclear; both are significant, so the conclusion is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The FA–SSRT correlation is printed as r = 0.24 without a sign, while the text and Fig. 1C describe higher FA with shorter SSRT, a negative relation; R² is labelled the linear correlation constant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction has to be taken from the text and the figure; the value is internally consistent (0.24 squared is 0.058, printed 0.057).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports abnormalities in fronto-striatal systems in both siblings, but the grey-matter clusters shared by both (Fig. 2C) are in the left amygdala, putamen, postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula; the only frontal finding is white matter beside the right inferior frontal gyrus.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's summary is broader than the shared grey-matter findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The main report says the medial temporal lobe and basal ganglia were enlarged in the sibling pairs, but the shared medial temporal cluster in Fig. 2C is the left amygdala only, and its enlargement failed the familiality test (P = 0.144). The supplement labels the same cluster amygdala/hippocampus in its text and Table S3 but amygdala in Table S2 and Fig. S1.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 602–603; pp. 5–6, 9–10 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: The hippocampal enlargement shared by both siblings that London et al. (2015) describe may come from the supplement's label, which is inconsistent within the supplement; no separate hippocampal cluster is reported anywhere.

reporting_issues.issue: Six familiality permutation tests are reported without correction for multiple testing, and the supplement shows that they are one-tailed (SOM p. 5).
reporting_issues.page: pp. 602–603; p. 5 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation: at a Bonferroni threshold of P < 0.0083 for six tests, the SSRT (0.033), putamen (0.013) and posterior insula (0.012) results would not be significant; only the two white-matter results (0.004) would.

reporting_issues.issue: The supplement describes the familiality test: the variance of within-pair differences in true pairs is compared with its distribution when each dependent participant is paired at random with an unrelated sibling (100,000 re-pairings, one-tailed; SOM p. 5). No removal of age, sex or other covariates before the test is described.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 602–603; p. 5 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: Siblings are likely to be closer in age than randomly paired participants (editors' reasoning, not stated in the paper), and age affects white-matter FA, grey-matter volume and stop-signal performance, so part of the familial similarity could be shared age or shared upbringing rather than shared genes; this adds to the genes-versus-environment limit already given.

reporting_issues.issue: The FA group difference F(2,141) = 26.3 is given for the skeleton of group differences (Fig. 1B legend, p. 602), and Table S2 confirms that its FA values are means over the 24,934 voxels that differed between groups; the right inferior frontal values used for the FA–SSRT regression come from the 317 such voxels inside the atlas region (none in the left inferior frontal gyrus) (SOM p. 9).
reporting_issues.page: p. 602; p. 9 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: The F, the editors' FA eta-squared of about 0.27 and the group differences in Table S2 are inflated by the selection of voxels for showing a group difference, and the pooled FA–SSRT correlation (r = 0.24) inherits both the voxel selection and the between-group difference.

reporting_issues.issue: After reporting that the grey-matter differences remained in non-smokers, the supplement says this result shows that the differences in siblings attributed to genetic risk might instead be attributable to environmental exposure to tobacco, the opposite of the paragraph's argument and of the main report's statement that tobacco is unlikely to explain the pattern (p. 603).
reporting_issues.page: p. 6 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: Almost certainly a wording error (the intended meaning, that tobacco does not explain the differences, is clear from the context and the main report); the sentence should not be cited as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The supplement's section on smoking is headed effects of tobacco smoking on gray and white matter, but only grey matter was re-analysed in non-smokers; no smoking analysis is reported for FA or SSRT, although 55% of siblings and 12% of controls smoked.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 5–6 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: The white-matter difference, the strongest familial result (P = 0.004), and the SSRT difference between siblings and controls may partly reflect smoking.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says tobacco-related grey-matter changes lie in prefrontal, cingulate and anterior insular cortex, and Table S3 that none of the tobacco-related regions was a candidate endophenotype; but Table S3 also lists tobacco-related findings in the superior temporal gyrus, postcentral gyrus and insula, the structures named for the third shared cluster, with peaks 26–34 mm from its peak, and a coordinate labelled left prefrontal cortex 15 mm from it (editors' calculation). Two coordinates labelled left prefrontal cortex have negative y values (−23 and −46), and one Brody et al. (2004) row is printed twice.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 5, 10 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: The anatomical argument that tobacco cannot explain the shared grey-matter differences is weaker than the text says; the non-smoker re-analysis, for grey matter only and without statistics, is the relevant evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The correlations of FA and grey matter with years of stimulant use (Fig. S2) are shown as maps only, without statistics, sample size, threshold or correction, and without adjustment for age or for other dependence; in this group years of use rise almost in step with age (onset 16.5, SD 2.8 years).
reporting_issues.page: pp. 2, 7 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: The main report's statement that white-matter changes can also result from drug-taking (p. 602) is not supported by reported statistics, and the maps may show effects of age, opiate or alcohol dependence rather than of stimulant use.

reporting_issues.issue: Table S1 reports the drug screening score (DAST-20) only for controls and non-dependent siblings, with F = 12.6, and gives no value for the dependent group; the 94% cocaine and 6% amphetamine figures are percentages without counts.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 2, 8 of the Supporting Online Material
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the dependent group's drug involvement is described by diagnoses only, and the counts must be inferred (3 of 50 with amphetamine dependence, editors' calculation).
